About the question text

Display of NCERT's exact wording is pending a copyright decision (Decision Log T14). Each item shows its textbook location and a prompt that is paraphrased where possible; word equations, equations and answer options are reproduced as given, because changing them would change the question. Students should read the full question in their NCERT book.

How every solution is laid out: Given / Asked → Concept used (and why it applies here) → Steps, one per line, with the reason in words → Check → ✅ Final answer → Common trap. One-mark MCQs use a compact form: Asked → Concept → Reasoning for each option → Answer.

Intext questions — page 6 (after §1.1)

Intext p.6, Q1Why clean a magnesium ribbon before burning it?2 marks

Given: a magnesium ribbon that is rubbed with sandpaper before it is burnt. Asked: the reason for cleaning it.

Concept used: magnesium is a reactive metal that slowly combines with air even at room temperature. Why it applies: a ribbon stored in air for some time is no longer pure magnesium on the outside.

  1. 1

    Magnesium kept in air slowly reacts with oxygen (and carbon dioxide) in the air.

  2. 2

    This forms a thin, dull white coating of magnesium oxide (and some magnesium carbonate) on its surface.

  3. 3

    This coating does not burn, so it shields the metal underneath and makes the ribbon hard to light.

  4. 4

    Rubbing with sandpaper removes the coating.

  5. 5

    Fresh, shiny magnesium is now in direct contact with oxygen, so it catches fire and burns easily.

  6. Check: a cleaned ribbon looks shiny; an old ribbon looks dull grey-white. The dull layer is the coating we removed, so the reason makes sense.

  7. Answer To remove the layer of magnesium oxide (and carbonate) formed on its surface by reaction with air. This layer stops the magnesium from burning; cleaning exposes fresh metal, which burns readily in oxygen.

    Common trap: Writing "to remove dust". The point is a chemical coating (an oxide layer), not dirt.
Intext p.6, Q2Write balanced equations for three word equations3 marks

Prompts: (i) hydrogen + chlorine → hydrogen chloride; (ii) barium chloride + aluminium sulphate → barium sulphate + aluminium chloride; (iii) sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen.

Given: three word equations. Asked: a balanced chemical equation for each.

Concept used: write correct formulae from valencies (Topic 2), then balance by hit-and-trial (Topic 3), changing only coefficients. Why it applies: a word equation must first become a skeletal equation; balancing then makes it obey the law of conservation of mass.

  1. 1

    (i) Hydrogen + chlorine → hydrogen chloride

    Hydrogen and chlorine gases are diatomic, so write HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ and ClX2\ce{Cl2}ClX2​.

  2. 2

    Hydrogen chloride: H (valency 1) and Cl (valency 1) → HCl\ce{HCl}HCl.

  3. 3

    Skeletal: HX2+ClX2→HCl\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> HCl}HX2​+ClX2​​HCl. Count: H 2 | 1, Cl 2 | 1.

  4. 4

    Both H and Cl are short by one on the right, so put 2 in front of HCl\ce{HCl}HCl. Now H 2 | 2 and Cl 2 | 2.

    HX2+ClX2→2 HCl\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}HX2​+ClX2​​2HClSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 1

    (ii) Barium chloride + aluminium sulphate → barium sulphate + aluminium chloride

    Barium chloride: Ba (2) and Cl (1) → BaClX2\ce{BaCl2}BaClX2​.

  6. 2

    Aluminium sulphate: Al (3) and SOX4\ce{SO4}SOX4​ (2) → criss-cross → AlX2(SOX4)X3\ce{Al2(SO4)3}AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​.

  7. 3

    Barium sulphate: Ba (2) and SOX4\ce{SO4}SOX4​ (2) → simplify → BaSOX4\ce{BaSO4}BaSOX4​.

  8. 4

    Aluminium chloride: Al (3) and Cl (1) → AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​.

  9. 5

    Skeletal: BaClX2+AlX2(SOX4)X3→BaSOX4+AlClX3\ce{BaCl2 + Al2(SO4)3 -> BaSO4 + AlCl3}BaClX2​+AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​​BaSOX4​+AlClX3​.

  10. 6

    Sulphate blocks: 3 on the left, 1 on the right → put 3 in front of BaSOX4\ce{BaSO4}BaSOX4​.

  11. 7

    Barium: now 3 on the right, 1 on the left → put 3 in front of BaClX2\ce{BaCl2}BaClX2​.

  12. 8

    Aluminium: 2 on the left, 1 on the right → put 2 in front of AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​.

  13. 9

    Chlorine: left 3 × 2 = 6; right 2 × 3 = 6 → already equal.

    3 BaClX2+AlX2(SOX4)X3→3 BaSOX4+2 AlClX3\ce{3BaCl2 + Al2(SO4)3 -> 3BaSO4 + 2AlCl3}3BaClX2​+AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​​3BaSOX4​+2AlClX3​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  14. 1

    (iii) Sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen

    Formulae: Na\ce{Na}Na, HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O, NaOH\ce{NaOH}NaOH, HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ (hydrogen gas is diatomic).

  15. 2

    Skeletal: Na+HX2O→NaOH+HX2\ce{Na + H2O -> NaOH + H2}Na+HX2​O​NaOH+HX2​. Hydrogen: 2 on the left, 1 + 2 = 3 on the right (odd).

  16. 3

    Make the right side even: put 2 in front of NaOH\ce{NaOH}NaOH. Right-side H = 2 + 2 = 4.

  17. 4

    Left-side H must be 4: put 2 in front of HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O. This also makes O 2 | 2.

  18. 5

    Sodium: 1 on the left, 2 on the right → put 2 in front of Na\ce{Na}Na.

    2 Na+2 HX2O→2 NaOH+HX2\ce{2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2}2Na+2HX2​O​2NaOH+HX2​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  19. Check: (i) H 2 | 2, Cl 2 | 2. (ii) Ba 3 | 3, Cl 6 | 6, Al 2 | 2, S 3 | 3, O 12 | 12. (iii) Na 2 | 2, H 4 | 4, O 2 | 2 ✔.

  20. Answer (i) HX2+ClX2→2 HCl\ce{H2 + Cl2 -> 2HCl}HX2​+ClX2​​2HCl (ii) 3 BaClX2+AlX2(SOX4)X3→3 BaSOX4+2 AlClX3\ce{3BaCl2 + Al2(SO4)3 -> 3BaSO4 + 2AlCl3}3BaClX2​+AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​​3BaSOX4​+2AlClX3​ (iii) 2 Na+2 HX2O→2 NaOH+HX2\ce{2Na + 2H2O -> 2NaOH + H2}2Na+2HX2​O​2NaOH+HX2​

    Common trap: In (ii), writing aluminium sulphate as AlSOX4\ce{AlSO4}AlSOX4​; in (i), writing hydrogen and chlorine as single atoms.
Intext p.6, Q3Balanced equations with state symbols3 marks

Prompts: (i) solutions of barium chloride and sodium sulphate react to give insoluble barium sulphate and sodium chloride solution; (ii) sodium hydroxide solution reacts with hydrochloric acid solution to give sodium chloride solution and water.

Given: two reactions described in words, including the state of each substance. Asked: balanced equations with state symbols.

Concept used: balance first, then read each state from the words — "solution / in water" → (aq), "insoluble" → (s), water itself → (l). Why it applies: the question gives the states in words, so we only translate them.

  1. 1

    (i)

    Skeletal: BaClX2+NaX2SOX4→BaSOX4+NaCl\ce{BaCl2 + Na2SO4 -> BaSO4 + NaCl}BaClX2​+NaX2​SOX4​​BaSOX4​+NaCl.

  2. 2

    Count: Na 2 | 1 and Cl 2 | 1.

  3. 3

    Put 2 in front of NaCl\ce{NaCl}NaCl; this fixes Na and Cl together.

  4. 4

    States: both reactants are solutions → (aq); barium sulphate is insoluble → (s); sodium chloride is a solution → (aq).

    BaClX2(aq)+NaX2SOX4(aq)→BaSOX4(s)+2 NaCl(aq)\ce{BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}BaClX2​(aq)+NaX2​SOX4​(aq)​BaSOX4​(s)+2NaCl(aq)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 1

    (ii)

    Skeletal: NaOH+HCl→NaCl+HX2O\ce{NaOH + HCl -> NaCl + H2O}NaOH+HCl​NaCl+HX2​O.

  6. 2

    Count: Na 1 | 1, O 1 | 1, H 1 + 1 = 2 | 2, Cl 1 | 1 → already balanced.

  7. 3

    States: the reactants are solutions → (aq); sodium chloride is a solution → (aq); water is a liquid → (l).

    NaOH(aq)+HCl(aq)→NaCl(aq)+HX2O(l)\ce{NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)}NaOH(aq)+HCl(aq)​NaCl(aq)+HX2​O(l)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  8. Check: (i) Ba 1 | 1, Cl 2 | 2, Na 2 | 2, S 1 | 1, O 4 | 4. (ii) Na, O, Cl 1 | 1; H 2 | 2 ✔. The only (s) in (i) is the substance called "insoluble" ✔.

  9. Answer (i) BaClX2(aq)+NaX2SOX4(aq)→BaSOX4(s)+2 NaCl(aq)\ce{BaCl2(aq) + Na2SO4(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}BaClX2​(aq)+NaX2​SOX4​(aq)​BaSOX4​(s)+2NaCl(aq) (ii) NaOH(aq)+HCl(aq)→NaCl(aq)+HX2O(l)\ce{NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)}NaOH(aq)+HCl(aq)​NaCl(aq)+HX2​O(l)

    Common trap: Writing HX2O(aq)\ce{H2O(aq)}HX2​O(aq) — water is the solvent itself, so it is (l).

Intext questions — page 10 (after §1.2.2)

Intext p.10, Q1Substance X used for whitewashing2 marks

Prompt: a solution of substance X is used for whitewashing. (i) Name X and give its formula. (ii) Write its reaction with water.

Given: X is used (as a solution) for whitewashing and reacts with water. Asked: name and formula of X; its reaction with water.

Concept used: quicklime reacts with water to form slaked lime, whose solution is brushed on walls (Topic 4). Why it applies: part (ii) asks for X's reaction with water, so X must be the substance that painters mix with water — quicklime.

  1. 1

    Painters buy quicklime, add water to it, and use the result to whitewash.

  2. 2

    So X is calcium oxide (quicklime).

  3. 3

    Its formula: Ca (valency 2) and O (valency 2) → CaO\ce{CaO}CaO.

  4. 4

    With water it combines to form calcium hydroxide (slaked lime) and gives out heat.

    CaO(s)+HX2O(l)→Ca(OH)X2(aq)+heat\ce{CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq)} + \text{heat}CaO(s)+HX2​O(l)​Ca(OH)X2​(aq)+heatSwipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: Ca 1 | 1, O 2 | 2, H 2 | 2 ✔. The product, slaked lime, is indeed what goes on the wall ✔.

  6. Answer (i) X = calcium oxide (quicklime), CaO\ce{CaO}CaO. (ii) CaO(s)+HX2O(l)→Ca(OH)X2(aq)\ce{CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq)}CaO(s)+HX2​O(l)​Ca(OH)X2​(aq) + heat.

    Note on wording: strictly, the solution brushed on walls is slaked lime, Ca(OH)X2\ce{Ca(OH)2}Ca(OH)X2​, made from X. Writing both names with the equation earns full marks.

    Common trap: Giving X as CaCOX3\ce{CaCO3}CaCOX3​ — that is the calcium carbonate that forms on the wall later.
Intext p.10, Q2Why is one gas volume double the other in the electrolysis of water? Name the gas.2 marks

Given: in the electrolysis of water, one test tube collects twice as much gas as the other. Asked: why, and which gas it is.

Concept used: electrolysis decomposes water into hydrogen and oxygen; the ratio comes from the formula HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O (Topic 5). Why it applies: both gases come only from water, so their amounts are fixed by water's formula.

  1. 1

    Electrolysis splits water:

    2 HX2O(l)→electric current2 HX2(g)+OX2(g)\ce{2H2O(l) ->[\text{electric current}] 2H2(g) + O2(g)}2HX2​O(l)electric current​2HX2​(g)+OX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Each water molecule contains 2 hydrogen atoms for every 1 oxygen atom.

  3. 3

    So the balanced equation gives 2 molecules of HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ for every 1 molecule of OX2\ce{O2}OX2​.

  4. 4

    Under the same conditions, twice the number of gas molecules takes up twice the volume.

  5. 5

    So the gas with double the volume is hydrogen, collected at the cathode.

  6. Check: volume ratio HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ : OX2\ce{O2}OX2​ = 2 : 1, the same as the coefficients 2 and 1 in the equation ✔.

  7. Answer The gas is hydrogen. Water contains hydrogen and oxygen atoms in the ratio 2 : 1, so electrolysis gives two volumes of hydrogen for every one volume of oxygen.

    Common trap: "Because hydrogen is lighter." Mass has nothing to do with it.

Intext questions — page 13 (after §1.3)

Intext p.13, Q1Why does copper sulphate solution change colour when an iron nail is dipped in it?2 marks

Given: an iron nail in blue copper sulphate solution; the colour changes. Asked: the reason.

Concept used: displacement — a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive metal from its compound (Topic 6). Why it applies: a free metal (iron) is placed in a solution of a compound of a different metal (copper).

  1. 1

    Copper sulphate solution is blue.

  2. 2

    Iron is more reactive than copper (it is higher on the reactivity ladder).

  3. 3

    So iron displaces copper from copper sulphate:

    Fe(s)+CuSOX4(aq)→FeSOX4(aq)+Cu(s)\ce{Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)}Fe(s)+CuSOX4​(aq)​FeSOX4​(aq)+Cu(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    As blue copper sulphate is used up, the blue colour fades.

  5. 5

    Iron(II) sulphate solution is pale green, so the solution turns light green.

  6. 6

    The displaced copper deposits on the nail as a reddish-brown coat.

  7. Check: the equation is balanced (Fe 1 | 1, Cu 1 | 1, SOX4\ce{SO4}SOX4​ 1 | 1) and both observations — fading blue and a brown coat — are explained ✔.

  8. Answer Iron, being more reactive than copper, displaces copper from copper sulphate. Blue copper sulphate changes into pale green iron sulphate, so the colour changes from blue to light green.

    Common trap: Saying "the nail rusts and colours the water". The brown coat is copper, and rust does not form in 20 minutes.
Intext p.13, Q2Another example of a double displacement reaction1 mark

Given: the textbook's example (sodium sulphate + barium chloride). Asked: a different double displacement reaction.

Concept used: double displacement — two compounds exchange ions (Topic 6). Why it applies: we need two compounds whose positive and negative parts swap partners.

  1. 1

    Choose two soluble compounds: lead nitrate and potassium iodide.

  2. 2

    Swap partners: lead pairs with iodide → lead iodide; potassium pairs with nitrate → potassium nitrate.

  3. 3

    Formulae: PbIX2\ce{PbI2}PbIX2​ (Pb valency 2, I valency 1) and KNOX3\ce{KNO3}KNOX3​.

  4. 4

    Iodide: 2 needed on the left → 2 KI\ce{2KI}2KI.

  5. 5

    Nitrate: 2 on the left → 2 KNOX3\ce{2KNO3}2KNOX3​ on the right.

    Pb(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 KI(aq)→PbIX2(s)+2 KNOX3(aq)\ce{Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)}Pb(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2KI(aq)​PbIX2​(s)+2KNOX3​(aq)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: Pb 1 | 1, N 2 | 2, O 6 | 6, K 2 | 2, I 2 | 2 ✔. Both reactants are compounds and each product contains one part from each reactant — a true swap ✔.

  7. Answer Pb(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 KI(aq)→PbIX2(s)+2 KNOX3(aq)\ce{Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)}Pb(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2KI(aq)​PbIX2​(s)+2KNOX3​(aq) (yellow precipitate of lead iodide). Other correct examples: AgNOX3(aq)+NaCl(aq)→AgCl(s)+NaNOX3(aq)\ce{AgNO3(aq) + NaCl(aq) -> AgCl(s) + NaNO3(aq)}AgNOX3​(aq)+NaCl(aq)​AgCl(s)+NaNOX3​(aq); NaOH(aq)+HCl(aq)→NaCl(aq)+HX2O(l)\ce{NaOH(aq) + HCl(aq) -> NaCl(aq) + H2O(l)}NaOH(aq)+HCl(aq)​NaCl(aq)+HX2​O(l).

    Common trap: Giving a displacement example such as Zn+CuSOX4\ce{Zn + CuSO4}Zn+CuSOX4​ — a free element takes part, so it is not double displacement.
Intext p.13, Q3Identify the substances oxidised and reduced2 marks

Prompts: (i) 4 Na(s)+OX2(g)→2 NaX2O(s)\ce{4Na(s) + O2(g) -> 2Na2O(s)}4Na(s)+OX2​(g)​2NaX2​O(s) (ii) CuO(s)+HX2(g)→Cu(s)+HX2O(l)\ce{CuO(s) + H2(g) -> Cu(s) + H2O(l)}CuO(s)+HX2​(g)​Cu(s)+HX2​O(l)

Given: two balanced equations. Asked: the substance oxidised and the substance reduced in each.

Concept used: oxidation = gain of oxygen (or loss of hydrogen); reduction = loss of oxygen (or gain of hydrogen) (Topic 7). Why it applies: in both reactions oxygen moves from one reactant to another, so we can follow it.

  1. 1

    (i)

    Sodium (Na) becomes sodium oxide (NaX2O\ce{Na2O}NaX2​O): sodium gains oxygen → sodium is oxidised.

  2. 2

    Oxygen gas supplies that oxygen; oxidation and reduction always occur together → oxygen is reduced.

  3. 1

    (ii)

    CuO\ce{CuO}CuO becomes Cu: copper(II) oxide loses oxygen → CuO\ce{CuO}CuO is reduced.

  4. 2

    HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ becomes HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O: hydrogen gains oxygen → hydrogen is oxidised.

  5. Check: in each reaction we found one substance oxidised and one reduced — as every redox reaction must have ✔.

  6. Answer (i) Oxidised: Na; reduced: OX2\ce{O2}OX2​. (ii) Oxidised: HX2\ce{H2}HX2​; reduced: CuO\ce{CuO}CuO.

    Note for (i): the key mark is "sodium is oxidised". (Beyond the syllabus: the full explanation of oxygen being reduced uses electron transfer, taught in Class 11.)

    Common trap: In (ii), writing "copper is reduced". Copper is the product; copper oxide is what was reduced.

In-text prompts and activity questions

Prompt (p.5)Balance Equation 1.2, Mg+OX2→MgO\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}Mg+OX2​​MgO1 mark

Given: the skeletal equation Mg+OX2→MgO\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO}Mg+OX2​​MgO. Asked: the balanced equation.

Concept used: hit-and-trial balancing; change only coefficients. Why it applies: the formulae are already correct; only the numbers of particles must change.

  1. 1

    Count: Mg 1 | 1; O 2 | 1. Oxygen is short on the right.

  2. 2

    Put 2 in front of MgO\ce{MgO}MgO → O 2 | 2, but now Mg 1 | 2.

  3. 3

    Put 2 in front of Mg → Mg 2 | 2.

  4. Check: Mg 2 | 2; O 2 | 2 ✔.

  5. Answer 2 Mg+OX2→2 MgO\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}2Mg+OX2​​2MgO

    Common trap: Writing Mg+OX2→MgOX2\ce{Mg + O2 -> MgO2}Mg+OX2​​MgOX2​ — that changes the formula of magnesium oxide.
Prompt (p.7)Type of reaction when magnesium burns (one product, heat given out)1 mark

Given: magnesium burns in air to give only magnesium oxide, and heat is given out. Asked: the type of reaction.

Concept used: combination (one product) and exothermic (heat given out). Why it applies: the prompt itself tells us there is one product and that heat is released.

  1. 1

    Reactants: magnesium and oxygen — two substances.

  2. 2

    Product: magnesium oxide only — one substance → combination.

  3. 3

    Heat and light are given out → exothermic.

    2 Mg(s)+OX2(g)→2 MgO(s)\ce{2Mg(s) + O2(g) -> 2MgO(s)}2Mg(s)+OX2​(g)​2MgO(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: two reactants → one product matches the definition of combination ✔.

  5. Answer A combination reaction that is also exothermic (and, as you learn in Topic 7, magnesium is oxidised).

    Common trap: Answering only "exothermic". The prompt asks for the type, which is combination.
Prompt (p.10)Barium hydroxide + ammonium chloride: what do you feel? Exothermic or endothermic?2 marks

Given: solid barium hydroxide and ammonium chloride are mixed in a test tube held in your palm. Asked: what you feel; exothermic or endothermic.

Concept used: heat flows from a warmer body to a cooler one; a reaction that takes in heat from its surroundings is endothermic (Topic 5). Why it applies: your palm is the "surroundings" of the reaction.

  1. 1

    When the solids are mixed, the bottom of the test tube feels cold — strongly enough that moisture from the air may condense or even freeze on the outside.

  2. 2

    Feeling cold means heat is flowing from your palm into the test tube.

  3. 3

    So the reaction is absorbing heat from its surroundings.

  4. 4

    A reaction that absorbs heat is endothermic.

  5. 5

    A smell of ammonia may also be noticed. The reaction is:

    Ba(OH)X2(s)+2 NHX4Cl(s)→BaClX2(aq)+2 NHX3(g)+2 HX2O(l)\ce{Ba(OH)2(s) + 2NH4Cl(s) -> BaCl2(aq) + 2NH3(g) + 2H2O(l)}Ba(OH)X2​(s)+2NHX4​Cl(s)​BaClX2​(aq)+2NHX3​(g)+2HX2​O(l)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: Ba 1 | 1, O 2 | 2, H 10 | 10, N 2 | 2, Cl 2 | 2 ✔. "Cold" and "endothermic" agree ✔.

  7. Answer The test tube feels cold. The reaction absorbs heat, so it is endothermic.

    Note: the lab usually uses the crystalline form, barium hydroxide octahydrate; the water in its crystals is why a liquid forms. (Beyond the syllabus.)

    Common trap: "It feels cold, so heat is given out to my hand." Cold means heat is leaving your hand.
Prompt (p.12)Recall Activity 1.2 (lead nitrate + potassium iodide): (i) colour and name of precipitate (ii) balanced equation (iii) double displacement?3 marks

Given: lead nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution. Asked: precipitate colour and name; balanced equation; whether it is double displacement.

Concept used: precipitation and double displacement (Topic 6). Why it applies: two solutions of compounds are mixed and a solid appears.

  1. 1

    (i) A bright yellow solid forms; it is lead iodide, PbIX2\ce{PbI2}PbIX2​.

  2. 2

    (ii) Lead (valency 2) pairs with iodide (valency 1) → PbIX2\ce{PbI2}PbIX2​; potassium pairs with nitrate → KNOX3\ce{KNO3}KNOX3​.

  3. 3

    Iodide: 2 needed → 2 KI\ce{2KI}2KI.

  4. 4

    Nitrate: 2 on the left → 2 KNOX3\ce{2KNO3}2KNOX3​.

    Pb(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 KI(aq)→PbIX2(s)+2 KNOX3(aq)\ce{Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)}Pb(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2KI(aq)​PbIX2​(s)+2KNOX3​(aq)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    (iii) Both reactants are compounds and they exchange ions → yes, double displacement (and also precipitation).

  6. Check: Pb 1 | 1, N 2 | 2, O 6 | 6, K 2 | 2, I 2 | 2 ✔.

  7. Answer (i) Yellow; lead iodide. (ii) Pb(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 KI(aq)→PbIX2(s)+2 KNOX3(aq)\ce{Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)}Pb(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2KI(aq)​PbIX2​(s)+2KNOX3​(aq) (iii) Yes — ions are exchanged.

    Common trap: Naming the yellow solid "potassium nitrate". Potassium nitrate stays dissolved; lead iodide is the insoluble product.
Prompt (p.10)What form of energy causes the decomposition of silver chloride and silver bromide?1 mark

Given: silver chloride and silver bromide decompose when kept in sunlight. Asked: the form of energy.

Concept used: decomposition is named by the energy that drives it (Topic 5). Why it applies: nothing is heated and no current is passed — only sunlight is present.

  1. 1

    Both reactions happen only when the salts are kept in sunlight.

  2. 2

    So the energy is supplied as light.

    2 AgCl(s)→sunlight2 Ag(s)+ClX2(g)2 AgBr(s)→sunlight2 Ag(s)+BrX2(g)\ce{2AgCl(s) ->[\text{sunlight}] 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)}\qquad \ce{2AgBr(s) ->[\text{sunlight}] 2Ag(s) + Br2(g)}2AgCl(s)sunlight​2Ag(s)+ClX2​(g)2AgBr(s)sunlight​2Ag(s)+BrX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  3. Check: in the dark these salts stay unchanged — which is why they are stored in dark bottles ✔.

  4. Answer Light energy (sunlight). These are photolytic decomposition reactions.

    In the lab…

    bromine is actually a red-brown liquid at room temperature, so BrX2(l)\ce{Br2(l)}BrX2​(l) would be more accurate. The textbook writes BrX2(g)\ce{Br2(g)}BrX2​(g); write it the textbook's way in the exam.

Prompt (p.13)When magnesium burns to form magnesium oxide, is magnesium oxidised or reduced?1 mark

Given: 2 Mg+OX2→2 MgO\ce{2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO}2Mg+OX2​​2MgO. Asked: oxidised or reduced?

Concept used: oxidation = gain of oxygen (Topic 7). Why it applies: magnesium joins with oxygen.

  1. 1

    Mg becomes MgO\ce{MgO}MgO — magnesium gains oxygen.

  2. 2

    Gain of oxygen is oxidation.

  3. Check: the oxygen comes from the air, so another substance (oxygen gas) is reduced — oxidation is paired with reduction ✔.

  4. Answer Magnesium is oxidised.

    Common trap: Thinking a "burning" metal is "reduced" because it gets smaller. Size has nothing to do with it.

End-of-chapter Exercises

Exercise Q1Which statements about 2 PbO(s)+C(s)→2 Pb(s)+COX2(g)\ce{2PbO(s) + C(s) -> 2Pb(s) + CO2(g)}2PbO(s)+C(s)​2Pb(s)+COX2​(g) are incorrect?MCQ1 mark

Statements: (a) lead is getting reduced; (b) carbon dioxide is getting oxidised; (c) carbon is getting oxidised; (d) lead oxide is getting reduced.

Choose your answer first — the full solution opens after.

contains exactly the two incorrect statements
includes (c), which is correct
includes
includes

Asked: the incorrect statements.

Concept used: name the reactant that gains or loses oxygen (Topic 7, worked example 4) — oxidation and reduction describe what happens to starting substances.

  1. 1

    Reasoning, statement by statement:

    (d) PbO\ce{PbO}PbO → Pb: lead oxide loses oxygen → reduced. Correct statement.

  2. 2

    (c) C → COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​: carbon gains oxygen → oxidised. Correct statement.

  3. 3

    (a) "Lead is reduced": lead is a product; the substance that lost oxygen is lead oxide. Incorrect.

  4. 4

    (b) "Carbon dioxide is oxidised": COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ is a product, not something that reacts here. Incorrect.

    Options: (i) contains exactly the two incorrect statements ✔. (ii) includes (c), which is correct ✘. (iii) includes (c) ✘. (iv) includes (c) and (d) ✘.

  5. Answer (i) (a) and (b)

    Common trap: Thinking "lead is reduced" sounds right. It is lead oxide that is reduced.
Exercise Q2FeX2OX3+2 Al→AlX2OX3+2 Fe\ce{Fe2O3 + 2Al -> Al2O3 + 2Fe}FeX2​OX3​+2Al​AlX2​OX3​+2Fe is an example of which type of reaction?MCQ1 mark

Choose your answer first — the full solution opens after.

Combination needs one product; there are two (AlX2OX3\ce{Al2O3}AlX2​OX3​, Fe)
Double displacement needs two compounds swapping partners; aluminium is a free element
Decomposition needs one reactant; there are two
Free aluminium takes iron's place in iron oxide, and iron comes out free → displacement

Asked: the type of reaction.

Concept used: the "Which type is it?" routine — count products and reactants, then look for a free element.

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) Combination needs one product; there are two (AlX2OX3\ce{Al2O3}AlX2​OX3​, Fe) ✘.
    • (c) Decomposition needs one reactant; there are two ✘.
    • (b) Double displacement needs two compounds swapping partners; aluminium is a free element ✘.
    • (d) Free aluminium takes iron's place in iron oxide, and iron comes out free → displacement ✔.

  2. Check: Fe 2 | 2, O 3 | 3, Al 2 | 2 — the equation is balanced as given ✔.

  3. Answer (d) displacement reaction.

    Extra (useful for exams): this is the thermit reaction, used to weld railway tracks. It is also redox: FeX2OX3\ce{Fe2O3}FeX2​OX3​ is reduced and Al is oxidised.
Exercise Q3What happens when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to iron filings?MCQ1 mark

Choose your answer first — the full solution opens after.

Iron is above hydrogen → it displaces hydrogen, forming iron chloride and hydrogen gas
Chlorine stays combined (as chloride); no hydroxide can form because no base is present
Iron is reactive enough to react with dilute acid
Salt + water forms when an acid reacts with a base, not with a metal

Asked: the products of iron + dilute hydrochloric acid.

Concept used: a metal above hydrogen on the reactivity ladder displaces hydrogen from a dilute acid (Topic 6).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) Iron is above hydrogen → it displaces hydrogen, forming iron chloride and hydrogen gas ✔.
    • (b) Chlorine stays combined (as chloride); no hydroxide can form because no base is present ✘.
    • (c) Iron is reactive enough to react with dilute acid ✘.
    • (d) Salt + water forms when an acid reacts with a base, not with a metal ✘.
    Fe(s)+2 HCl(aq)→FeClX2(aq)+HX2(g)\ce{Fe(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> FeCl2(aq) + H2(g)}Fe(s)+2HCl(aq)​FeClX2​(aq)+HX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  2. Check: Fe 1 | 1, H 2 | 2, Cl 2 | 2 ✔; bubbles of hydrogen are what you actually see ✔.

  3. Answer (a) Hydrogen gas and iron chloride are produced.

Exercise Q4What is a balanced chemical equation? Why should equations be balanced?2 marks

Given: — Asked: a definition and a reason.

Concept used: law of conservation of mass (Topic 3). Why it applies: balancing is how an equation shows that mass is conserved.

  1. 1

    Definition: a balanced chemical equation has the same number of atoms of each element on the reactant side and on the product side.

  2. 2

    Example: 2 HX2+OX2→2 HX2O\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}2HX2​+OX2​​2HX2​O has H 4 | 4 and O 2 | 2.

  3. 3

    Reason: by the law of conservation of mass, mass can neither be created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.

  4. 4

    In a reaction, atoms are only rearranged — none disappear and none appear.

  5. 5

    So the number of atoms of each element must be equal on both sides; only then does the equation show that mass is conserved.

  6. Check: in the example, the 4 H and 2 O atoms that go in are exactly the atoms that come out ✔.

  7. Answer A balanced equation has equal numbers of atoms of each element on both sides. Equations must be balanced to obey the law of conservation of mass — atoms are neither created nor destroyed in a reaction.

    Common trap: Saying "the number of molecules must be equal". Molecules can change in number (2 HX2+OX2\ce{2H2 + O2}2HX2​+OX2​ is 3 molecules; 2 HX2O\ce{2H2O}2HX2​O is 2); atoms cannot.
Exercise Q5Translate into chemical equations and balance4 marks

Prompts: (a) hydrogen gas combines with nitrogen to form ammonia; (b) hydrogen sulphide gas burns in air to give water and sulphur dioxide; (c) barium chloride reacts with aluminium sulphate to give aluminium chloride and a precipitate of barium sulphate; (d) potassium metal reacts with water to give potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.

Given: four statements in words. Asked: balanced chemical equations.

Concept used: words → correct formulae → hit-and-trial balancing (Topic 2, Topic 3). Why it applies: each statement names every reactant and product, so we can write a skeletal equation and then balance it.

  1. 1

    (a) Hydrogen + nitrogen → ammonia

    Both gases are diatomic: HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ and NX2\ce{N2}NX2​. Ammonia is NHX3\ce{NH3}NHX3​.

  2. 2

    Skeletal: NX2+HX2→NHX3\ce{N2 + H2 -> NH3}NX2​+HX2​​NHX3​. Count: N 2 | 1; H 2 | 3.

  3. 3

    Nitrogen: 2 on the left → put 2 in front of NHX3\ce{NH3}NHX3​. Now H on the right = 2 × 3 = 6.

  4. 4

    Hydrogen: 6 needed on the left → put 3 in front of HX2\ce{H2}HX2​.

    NX2(g)+3 HX2(g)→2 NHX3(g)\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) -> 2NH3(g)}NX2​(g)+3HX2​(g)​2NHX3​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 1

    (b) Hydrogen sulphide burns in air

    Formulae: HX2S\ce{H2S}HX2​S; oxygen from air OX2\ce{O2}OX2​; water HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O; sulphur dioxide SOX2\ce{SO2}SOX2​.

  6. 2

    Skeletal: HX2S+OX2→HX2O+SOX2\ce{H2S + O2 -> H2O + SO2}HX2​S+OX2​​HX2​O+SOX2​. Count: H 2 | 2; S 1 | 1; O 2 | 1 + 2 = 3.

  7. 3

    Oxygen is 3 (odd) on the right but always even on the left (from OX2\ce{O2}OX2​). Double both products: 2 HX2O+2 SOX2\ce{2H2O + 2SO2}2HX2​O+2SOX2​ → O on the right = 2 + 4 = 6.

  8. 4

    Hydrogen on the right is now 4 → put 2 in front of HX2S\ce{H2S}HX2​S (H 4 | 4; S 2 | 2).

  9. 5

    Oxygen on the left must be 6 → put 3 in front of OX2\ce{O2}OX2​.

    2 HX2S(g)+3 OX2(g)→2 HX2O(l)+2 SOX2(g)\ce{2H2S(g) + 3O2(g) -> 2H2O(l) + 2SO2(g)}2HX2​S(g)+3OX2​(g)​2HX2​O(l)+2SOX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  10. 1

    (c) Barium chloride + aluminium sulphate

    Formulae: BaClX2\ce{BaCl2}BaClX2​, AlX2(SOX4)X3\ce{Al2(SO4)3}AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​, AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​, BaSOX4\ce{BaSO4}BaSOX4​ (the precipitate).

  11. 2

    Skeletal: BaClX2+AlX2(SOX4)X3→AlClX3+BaSOX4\ce{BaCl2 + Al2(SO4)3 -> AlCl3 + BaSO4}BaClX2​+AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​​AlClX3​+BaSOX4​.

  12. 3

    Sulphate: 3 on the left, 1 on the right → put 3 in front of BaSOX4\ce{BaSO4}BaSOX4​.

  13. 4

    Barium: now 3 on the right → put 3 in front of BaClX2\ce{BaCl2}BaClX2​.

  14. 5

    Aluminium: 2 on the left → put 2 in front of AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​.

  15. 6

    Chlorine: left 3 × 2 = 6; right 2 × 3 = 6 → balanced.

    3 BaClX2(aq)+AlX2(SOX4)X3(aq)→2 AlClX3(aq)+3 BaSOX4(s)\ce{3BaCl2(aq) + Al2(SO4)3(aq) -> 2AlCl3(aq) + 3BaSO4(s)}3BaClX2​(aq)+AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​(aq)​2AlClX3​(aq)+3BaSOX4​(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  16. 1

    (d) Potassium + water

    Formulae: K (a metal, single symbol); HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O; KOH\ce{KOH}KOH (K valency 1, OH valency 1); HX2\ce{H2}HX2​.

  17. 2

    Skeletal: K+HX2O→KOH+HX2\ce{K + H2O -> KOH + H2}K+HX2​O​KOH+HX2​. Count: K 1 | 1; O 1 | 1; H 2 | 1 + 2 = 3 (odd).

  18. 3

    Make hydrogen on the right even: put 2 in front of KOH\ce{KOH}KOH → H on the right = 2 + 2 = 4.

  19. 4

    Hydrogen on the left must be 4 → put 2 in front of HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O (this also makes O 2 | 2).

  20. 5

    Potassium: now 2 on the right → put 2 in front of K.

    2 K(s)+2 HX2O(l)→2 KOH(aq)+HX2(g)\ce{2K(s) + 2H2O(l) -> 2KOH(aq) + H2(g)}2K(s)+2HX2​O(l)​2KOH(aq)+HX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  21. Check: (a) N 2 | 2, H 6 | 6. (b) H 4 | 4, S 2 | 2, O 6 | 6. (c) Ba 3 | 3, Cl 6 | 6, Al 2 | 2, S 3 | 3, O 12 | 12. (d) K 2 | 2, H 4 | 4, O 2 | 2 ✔.

  22. Answer (a) NX2+3 HX2→2 NHX3\ce{N2 + 3H2 -> 2NH3}NX2​+3HX2​​2NHX3​ (b) 2 HX2S+3 OX2→2 HX2O+2 SOX2\ce{2H2S + 3O2 -> 2H2O + 2SO2}2HX2​S+3OX2​​2HX2​O+2SOX2​ (c) 3 BaClX2+AlX2(SOX4)X3→2 AlClX3+3 BaSOX4\ce{3BaCl2 + Al2(SO4)3 -> 2AlCl3 + 3BaSO4}3BaClX2​+AlX2​(SOX4​)X3​​2AlClX3​+3BaSOX4​ (d) 2 K+2 HX2O→2 KOH+HX2\ce{2K + 2H2O -> 2KOH + H2}2K+2HX2​O​2KOH+HX2​

    Common trap: In (a), writing N+3 H→NHX3\ce{N + 3H -> NH3}N+3H​NHX3​. Both gases are diatomic.
Exercise Q6Balance the equations4 marks

Prompts: (a) HNOX3+Ca(OH)X2→Ca(NOX3)X2+HX2O\ce{HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + H2O}HNOX3​+Ca(OH)X2​​Ca(NOX3​)X2​+HX2​O (b) NaOH+HX2SOX4→NaX2SOX4+HX2O\ce{NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + H2O}NaOH+HX2​SOX4​​NaX2​SOX4​+HX2​O (c) NaCl+AgNOX3→AgCl+NaNOX3\ce{NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl + NaNO3}NaCl+AgNOX3​​AgCl+NaNOX3​ (d) BaClX2+HX2SOX4→BaSOX4+HCl\ce{BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + HCl}BaClX2​+HX2​SOX4​​BaSOX4​+HCl

Given: four skeletal equations. Asked: balance them.

Concept used: hit-and-trial; count unchanged polyatomic ions (NOX3\ce{NO3}NOX3​, SOX4\ce{SO4}SOX4​) as one block; count brackets correctly. Why it applies: in every equation the polyatomic group passes unchanged from one side to the other.

  1. 1

    (a)

    Nitrate blocks: left 1, right 2 (the subscript 2 outside the bracket) → put 2 in front of HNOX3\ce{HNO3}HNOX3​.

  2. 2

    Hydrogen: left 2 (in 2 HNOX3\ce{2HNO3}2HNOX3​) + 2 (in Ca(OH)X2\ce{Ca(OH)2}Ca(OH)X2​) = 4; right 2 → put 2 in front of HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O.

  3. 3

    Recount oxygen: left 6 + 2 = 8; right 6 + 2 = 8 ✔.

    2 HNOX3+Ca(OH)X2→Ca(NOX3)X2+2 HX2O\ce{2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O}2HNOX3​+Ca(OH)X2​​Ca(NOX3​)X2​+2HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 1

    (b)

    Sodium: left 1, right 2 → put 2 in front of NaOH\ce{NaOH}NaOH.

  5. 2

    Hydrogen: left 2 + 2 = 4; right 2 → put 2 in front of HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O.

  6. 3

    Recount oxygen: left 2 + 4 = 6; right 4 + 2 = 6 ✔.

    2 NaOH+HX2SOX4→NaX2SOX4+2 HX2O\ce{2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O}2NaOH+HX2​SOX4​​NaX2​SOX4​+2HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 1

    (c)

    Count: Na 1 | 1; Cl 1 | 1; Ag 1 | 1; nitrate 1 | 1.

  8. 2

    Every element already matches → the equation is already balanced; no coefficient is needed.

    NaCl+AgNOX3→AgCl+NaNOX3\ce{NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl + NaNO3}NaCl+AgNOX3​​AgCl+NaNOX3​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  9. 1

    (d)

    Count: Ba 1 | 1; sulphate 1 | 1; H 2 | 1; Cl 2 | 1.

  10. 2

    Put 2 in front of HCl\ce{HCl}HCl → H 2 | 2 and Cl 2 | 2.

    BaClX2+HX2SOX4→BaSOX4+2 HCl\ce{BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2HCl}BaClX2​+HX2​SOX4​​BaSOX4​+2HClSwipe to see the whole equation →

  11. Check: (a) Ca 1 | 1, N 2 | 2, O 8 | 8, H 4 | 4. (b) Na 2 | 2, S 1 | 1, O 6 | 6, H 4 | 4. (c) all 1 | 1. (d) Ba 1 | 1, S 1 | 1, O 4 | 4, H 2 | 2, Cl 2 | 2 ✔.

  12. Answer (a) 2 HNOX3+Ca(OH)X2→Ca(NOX3)X2+2 HX2O\ce{2HNO3 + Ca(OH)2 -> Ca(NO3)2 + 2H2O}2HNOX3​+Ca(OH)X2​​Ca(NOX3​)X2​+2HX2​O (b) 2 NaOH+HX2SOX4→NaX2SOX4+2 HX2O\ce{2NaOH + H2SO4 -> Na2SO4 + 2H2O}2NaOH+HX2​SOX4​​NaX2​SOX4​+2HX2​O (c) NaCl+AgNOX3→AgCl+NaNOX3\ce{NaCl + AgNO3 -> AgCl + NaNO3}NaCl+AgNOX3​​AgCl+NaNOX3​ (already balanced) (d) BaClX2+HX2SOX4→BaSOX4+2 HCl\ce{BaCl2 + H2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2HCl}BaClX2​+HX2​SOX4​​BaSOX4​+2HCl

    Common trap: In (c), adding coefficients to an equation that is already balanced — always count before changing anything. In (a), reading Ca(OH)X2\ce{Ca(OH)2}Ca(OH)X2​ as one O and one H.
Exercise Q7Write balanced equations from word equations4 marks

Prompts: (a) calcium hydroxide + carbon dioxide → calcium carbonate + water; (b) zinc + silver nitrate → zinc nitrate + silver; (c) aluminium + copper chloride → aluminium chloride + copper; (d) barium chloride + potassium sulphate → barium sulphate + potassium chloride.

Given: four word equations. Asked: balanced chemical equations.

Concept used: formulae from valencies (Topic 2), then hit-and-trial (Topic 3). Why it applies: only names are given, so formulae must be built first.

  1. 1

    (a)

    Formulae: Ca(OH)X2\ce{Ca(OH)2}Ca(OH)X2​, COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​, CaCOX3\ce{CaCO3}CaCOX3​, HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O.

  2. 2

    Count: Ca 1 | 1; C 1 | 1; H 2 | 2; O 2 + 2 = 4 | 3 + 1 = 4.

  3. 3

    All equal → already balanced.

    Ca(OH)X2+COX2→CaCOX3+HX2O\ce{Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O}Ca(OH)X2​+COX2​​CaCOX3​+HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 1

    (b)

    Formulae: Zn; AgNOX3\ce{AgNO3}AgNOX3​ (Ag 1, NOX3\ce{NO3}NOX3​ 1); Zn(NOX3)X2\ce{Zn(NO3)2}Zn(NOX3​)X2​ (Zn 2); Ag.

  5. 2

    Nitrate: left 1, right 2 → put 2 in front of AgNOX3\ce{AgNO3}AgNOX3​.

  6. 3

    Silver: left 2, right 1 → put 2 in front of Ag.

    Zn+2 AgNOX3→Zn(NOX3)X2+2 Ag\ce{Zn + 2AgNO3 -> Zn(NO3)2 + 2Ag}Zn+2AgNOX3​​Zn(NOX3​)X2​+2AgSwipe to see the whole equation →
  7. 1

    (c)

    Formulae: Al; CuClX2\ce{CuCl2}CuClX2​ (copper(II), valency 2); AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​ (Al valency 3); Cu.

  8. 2

    Chlorine: 2 on the left, 3 on the right. The smallest number both divide into is 6.

  9. 3

    Put 3 in front of CuClX2\ce{CuCl2}CuClX2​ (3 × 2 = 6 Cl).

  10. 4

    Put 2 in front of AlClX3\ce{AlCl3}AlClX3​ (2 × 3 = 6 Cl).

  11. 5

    Aluminium: now 2 on the right → put 2 in front of Al.

  12. 6

    Copper: now 3 on the left → put 3 in front of Cu.

    2 Al+3 CuClX2→2 AlClX3+3 Cu\ce{2Al + 3CuCl2 -> 2AlCl3 + 3Cu}2Al+3CuClX2​​2AlClX3​+3CuSwipe to see the whole equation →
  13. 1

    (d)

    Formulae: BaClX2\ce{BaCl2}BaClX2​, KX2SOX4\ce{K2SO4}KX2​SOX4​, BaSOX4\ce{BaSO4}BaSOX4​, KCl\ce{KCl}KCl.

  14. 2

    Potassium: left 2, right 1 → put 2 in front of KCl\ce{KCl}KCl. This also makes Cl 2 | 2.

    BaClX2+KX2SOX4→BaSOX4+2 KCl\ce{BaCl2 + K2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2KCl}BaClX2​+KX2​SOX4​​BaSOX4​+2KClSwipe to see the whole equation →

  15. Check: (a) all equal as shown. (b) Zn 1 | 1, Ag 2 | 2, N 2 | 2, O 6 | 6. (c) Al 2 | 2, Cu 3 | 3, Cl 6 | 6. (d) Ba 1 | 1, Cl 2 | 2, K 2 | 2, S 1 | 1, O 4 | 4 ✔.

  16. Answer (a) Ca(OH)X2+COX2→CaCOX3+HX2O\ce{Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O}Ca(OH)X2​+COX2​​CaCOX3​+HX2​O (b) Zn+2 AgNOX3→Zn(NOX3)X2+2 Ag\ce{Zn + 2AgNO3 -> Zn(NO3)2 + 2Ag}Zn+2AgNOX3​​Zn(NOX3​)X2​+2Ag (c) 2 Al+3 CuClX2→2 AlClX3+3 Cu\ce{2Al + 3CuCl2 -> 2AlCl3 + 3Cu}2Al+3CuClX2​​2AlClX3​+3Cu (d) BaClX2+KX2SOX4→BaSOX4+2 KCl\ce{BaCl2 + K2SO4 -> BaSO4 + 2KCl}BaClX2​+KX2​SOX4​​BaSOX4​+2KCl

    Common trap: In (c), writing copper chloride as CuCl\ce{CuCl}CuCl. Copper here is copper(II), valency 2 → CuClX2\ce{CuCl2}CuClX2​.
Exercise Q8Write balanced equations and identify the type of reaction4 marks

Prompts: (a) potassium bromide(aq) + barium iodide(aq) → potassium iodide(aq) + barium bromide(s); (b) zinc carbonate(s) → zinc oxide(s) + carbon dioxide(g); (c) hydrogen(g) + chlorine(g) → hydrogen chloride(g); (d) magnesium(s) + hydrochloric acid(aq) → magnesium chloride(aq) + hydrogen(g).

Given: four word equations with states. Asked: balanced equations and the type of each reaction.

Concept used: balancing (Topic 3) and the "Which type is it?" routine (wrap-up). Why it applies: each reaction must first be written correctly; its type is then read from the pattern of reactants and products.

  1. 1

    (a)

    Formulae: KBr\ce{KBr}KBr (K 1, Br 1); BaIX2\ce{BaI2}BaIX2​ (Ba 2, I 1); KI\ce{KI}KI; BaBrX2\ce{BaBr2}BaBrX2​.

  2. 2

    Skeletal: KBr+BaIX2→KI+BaBrX2\ce{KBr + BaI2 -> KI + BaBr2}KBr+BaIX2​​KI+BaBrX2​. Count: Br 1 | 2; I 2 | 1.

  3. 3

    Bromine: put 2 in front of KBr\ce{KBr}KBr → Br 2 | 2.

  4. 4

    Iodine: put 2 in front of KI\ce{KI}KI → I 2 | 2. Potassium: 2 | 2 ✔.

    2 KBr(aq)+BaIX2(aq)→2 KI(aq)+BaBrX2(s)\ce{2KBr(aq) + BaI2(aq) -> 2KI(aq) + BaBr2(s)}2KBr(aq)+BaIX2​(aq)​2KI(aq)+BaBrX2​(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Type: two compounds exchange ions (potassium moves from bromide to iodide; barium from iodide to bromide) → double displacement.

    Teacher's note (accuracy)

    The textbook marks barium bromide as a solid (s), i.e. a precipitate. In reality, barium bromide is very soluble in water (about 92 g dissolves in 100 mL of water at 0 °C), and so are KBr, BaIX2\ce{BaI2}BaIX2​ and KI. Mixing these two solutions would not produce any visible precipitate or change. For the exam, write the equation with the state symbols as given and classify it as double displacement — that is what the answer key expects. Just remember that this is a "paper" example, not something you would see in the lab.

  6. 1

    (b)

    Formulae: ZnCOX3\ce{ZnCO3}ZnCOX3​, ZnO\ce{ZnO}ZnO, COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​.

  7. 2

    Count: Zn 1 | 1; C 1 | 1; O 3 | 1 + 2 = 3 → already balanced.

    ZnCOX3(s)→heatZnO(s)+COX2(g)\ce{ZnCO3(s) ->[\text{heat}] ZnO(s) + CO2(g)}ZnCOX3​(s)heat​ZnO(s)+COX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  8. 3

    Type: one reactant → two products, broken down by heating → thermal decomposition.

  9. 1

    (c)

    Formulae: HX2\ce{H2}HX2​, ClX2\ce{Cl2}ClX2​ (diatomic), HCl\ce{HCl}HCl.

  10. 2

    Put 2 in front of HCl\ce{HCl}HCl → H 2 | 2, Cl 2 | 2.

    HX2(g)+ClX2(g)→2 HCl(g)\ce{H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g)}HX2​(g)+ClX2​(g)​2HCl(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  11. 3

    Type: two reactants → one product → combination.

  12. 1

    (d)

    Formulae: Mg; HCl\ce{HCl}HCl; MgClX2\ce{MgCl2}MgClX2​ (Mg 2, Cl 1); HX2\ce{H2}HX2​.

  13. 2

    Chlorine: left 1, right 2 → put 2 in front of HCl\ce{HCl}HCl. Hydrogen is then 2 | 2.

    Mg(s)+2 HCl(aq)→MgClX2(aq)+HX2(g)\ce{Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)}Mg(s)+2HCl(aq)​MgClX2​(aq)+HX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  14. 3

    Type: a free element (Mg) takes hydrogen's place in the acid, and hydrogen comes out free → displacement.

  15. Check: (a) K 2 | 2, Br 2 | 2, Ba 1 | 1, I 2 | 2. (b) as counted. (c) H 2 | 2, Cl 2 | 2. (d) Mg 1 | 1, H 2 | 2, Cl 2 | 2 ✔.

  16. Answer (a) 2 KBr(aq)+BaIX2(aq)→2 KI(aq)+BaBrX2(s)\ce{2KBr(aq) + BaI2(aq) -> 2KI(aq) + BaBr2(s)}2KBr(aq)+BaIX2​(aq)​2KI(aq)+BaBrX2​(s) — double displacement
    (b) ZnCOX3(s)→heatZnO(s)+COX2(g)\ce{ZnCO3(s) ->[\text{heat}] ZnO(s) + CO2(g)}ZnCOX3​(s)heat​ZnO(s)+COX2​(g) — decomposition (thermal)
    (c) HX2(g)+ClX2(g)→2 HCl(g)\ce{H2(g) + Cl2(g) -> 2HCl(g)}HX2​(g)+ClX2​(g)​2HCl(g) — combination
    (d) Mg(s)+2 HCl(aq)→MgClX2(aq)+HX2(g)\ce{Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) -> MgCl2(aq) + H2(g)}Mg(s)+2HCl(aq)​MgClX2​(aq)+HX2​(g) — displacement

    Common trap: In (d), calling it double displacement because HCl is a compound. Check for a free element first — Mg is one.
Exercise Q9What are exothermic and endothermic reactions? Give examples.3 marks

Given: — Asked: both definitions with examples.

Concept used: the direction in which energy flows between the reaction and its surroundings (Topic 4, Topic 5). Why it applies: the two words are defined by whether heat comes out or energy goes in.

  1. 1

    Exothermic reaction: a reaction that gives out heat to its surroundings as the products form; the surroundings get warmer.

  2. 2

    Examples:

    CaO(s)+HX2O(l)→Ca(OH)X2(aq)+heat\ce{CaO(s) + H2O(l) -> Ca(OH)2(aq)} + \text{heat}CaO(s)+HX2​O(l)​Ca(OH)X2​(aq)+heatSwipe to see the whole equation →
    CHX4(g)+2 OX2(g)→COX2(g)+2 HX2O(g)+heat\ce{CH4(g) + 2O2(g) -> CO2(g) + 2H2O(g)} + \text{heat}CHX4​(g)+2OX2​(g)​COX2​(g)+2HX2​O(g)+heatSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Endothermic reaction: a reaction that takes in energy (as heat, light or electricity); if it takes heat from the surroundings, they become colder.

  4. 4

    Examples:

    CaCOX3(s)→heatCaO(s)+COX2(g)\ce{CaCO3(s) ->[\text{heat}] CaO(s) + CO2(g)}CaCOX3​(s)heat​CaO(s)+COX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
    2 AgCl(s)→sunlight2 Ag(s)+ClX2(g)\ce{2AgCl(s) ->[\text{sunlight}] 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)}2AgCl(s)sunlight​2Ag(s)+ClX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: each example matches its definition — the first two need no continuous heating and warm their surroundings; the last two stop as soon as heat or light is removed ✔.

  6. Answer Exothermic = heat given out (e.g. quicklime + water; burning methane; respiration). Endothermic = energy absorbed (e.g. decomposition of calcium carbonate by heat; silver chloride in sunlight; photosynthesis).

    Common trap: Giving "melting ice" as an endothermic reaction. It absorbs heat, but it is a physical change, not a reaction.
Exercise Q10Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction?2 marks

Given: respiration in our cells. Asked: why it counts as exothermic.

Concept used: a reaction that releases energy is exothermic (Topic 4). Why it applies: respiration is how our body gets energy from food.

  1. 1

    During digestion, carbohydrates in food (rice, wheat, potatoes) are broken down into glucose.

  2. 2

    In our cells, glucose combines with the oxygen we breathe in.

  3. 3

    Carbon dioxide and water are formed and energy is released:

    CX6HX12OX6(aq)+6 OX2(aq)→6 COX2(aq)+6 HX2O(l)+energy\ce{C6H12O6(aq) + 6O2(aq) -> 6CO2(aq) + 6H2O(l)} + \text{energy}CX6​HX12​OX6​(aq)+6OX2​(aq)​6COX2​(aq)+6HX2​O(l)+energySwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Because energy is given out, respiration is exothermic.

  5. Check: this released energy is what keeps your body warm at about 37 °C — consistent with heat being given out ✔. (Equation: C 6 | 6, H 12 | 12, O 18 | 18 ✔.)

  6. Answer In respiration, glucose combines with oxygen in our cells to form carbon dioxide and water, and energy is released. Since energy is given out, respiration is exothermic.

    Common trap: Writing "because we breathe out warm air". Give the chemical reason — energy released when glucose reacts with oxygen.
Exercise Q11Why are decomposition reactions called the opposite of combination reactions? Write equations.3 marks

Given: — Asked: the reason, with equations.

Concept used: combination is many → one; decomposition is one → many (Topic 4, Topic 5). Why it applies: comparing the two patterns shows one is the reverse of the other.

  1. 1

    In a combination reaction, two or more substances join to form one product.

  2. 2

    In a decomposition reaction, one substance breaks down into two or more simpler substances.

  3. 3

    So the reactants of one are the products of the other — they are reverse processes.

  4. 4

    Energy also runs the opposite way: combination usually releases energy; decomposition usually absorbs it.

  5. 5

    Pair of equations:

    CaO(s)+COX2(g)→CaCOX3(s)(combination)\ce{CaO(s) + CO2(g) -> CaCO3(s)}\qquad\text{(combination)}CaO(s)+COX2​(g)​CaCOX3​(s)(combination)Swipe to see the whole equation →
    CaCOX3(s)→heatCaO(s)+COX2(g)(decomposition)\ce{CaCO3(s) ->[\text{heat}] CaO(s) + CO2(g)}\qquad\text{(decomposition)}CaCOX3​(s)heat​CaO(s)+COX2​(g)(decomposition)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: in the pair, the substances on the right of the first equation are exactly those on the left of the second ✔.

  7. Answer Combination: many → one. Decomposition: one → many. One is the reverse of the other, as the pair above shows. (Another pair: 2 HX2+OX2→2 HX2O\ce{2H2 + O2 -> 2H2O}2HX2​+OX2​​2HX2​O and, by electrolysis, 2 HX2O→2 HX2+OX2\ce{2H2O -> 2H2 + O2}2HX2​O​2HX2​+OX2​.)

    Common trap: Giving two unrelated equations. Use a pair with the same substances to show the reverse.
Exercise Q12One decomposition reaction each using heat, light and electricity3 marks

Given: — Asked: three equations, one for each energy source.

Concept used: thermal, photolytic and electrolytic decomposition (Topic 5). Why it applies: decomposition is named by the energy that breaks the compound.

  1. 1

    Heat (thermal decomposition):

    CaCOX3(s)→heatCaO(s)+COX2(g)\ce{CaCO3(s) ->[\text{heat}] CaO(s) + CO2(g)}CaCOX3​(s)heat​CaO(s)+COX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Light (photolytic decomposition):

    2 AgCl(s)→sunlight2 Ag(s)+ClX2(g)\ce{2AgCl(s) ->[\text{sunlight}] 2Ag(s) + Cl2(g)}2AgCl(s)sunlight​2Ag(s)+ClX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Electricity (electrolytic decomposition):

    2 HX2O(l)→electric current2 HX2(g)+OX2(g)\ce{2H2O(l) ->[\text{electric current}] 2H2(g) + O2(g)}2HX2​O(l)electric current​2HX2​(g)+OX2​(g)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: each has one reactant and two products (decomposition) and the correct energy written over the arrow; all are balanced ✔.

  5. Answer The three equations above. (Other correct choices: 2 FeSOX4→FeX2OX3+SOX2+SOX3\ce{2FeSO4 -> Fe2O3 + SO2 + SO3}2FeSOX4​​FeX2​OX3​+SOX2​+SOX3​ or 2 Pb(NOX3)X2→2 PbO+4 NOX2+OX2\ce{2Pb(NO3)2 -> 2PbO + 4NO2 + O2}2Pb(NOX3​)X2​​2PbO+4NOX2​+OX2​ for heat; 2 AgBr→2 Ag+BrX2\ce{2AgBr -> 2Ag + Br2}2AgBr​2Ag+BrX2​ for light.)

    Common trap: Naming the energy only in words without an equation — the question asks for equations.
Exercise Q13Difference between displacement and double displacement reactions, with equations3 marks

Given: — Asked: the difference, with one equation of each.

Concept used: the one-question test — is one reactant a free element? (Topic 6). Why it applies: this single feature separates the two types.

  1. 1

    Compare the two types:

    Displacement Double displacement
    A more reactive element displaces a less reactive element from its compound. Two compounds exchange ions (swap partners).
    One reactant is a free element. Both reactants are compounds.
    General form: A + BC → AC + B General form: AB + CD → AD + CB
    One element is set free. No free element appears.
  2. 2

    Displacement example:

    Fe(s)+CuSOX4(aq)→FeSOX4(aq)+Cu(s)\ce{Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)}Fe(s)+CuSOX4​(aq)​FeSOX4​(aq)+Cu(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Double displacement example:

    NaX2SOX4(aq)+BaClX2(aq)→BaSOX4(s)+2 NaCl(aq)\ce{Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}NaX2​SOX4​(aq)+BaClX2​(aq)​BaSOX4​(s)+2NaCl(aq)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: example 2 has a free element (Fe) among the reactants; example 3 has only compounds that swap partners ✔.

  5. Answer The table above, with one balanced equation of each type.

    Common trap: Writing "double displacement means two elements are displaced". It means two ions are exchanged between two compounds.
Exercise Q14Recovery of silver from silver nitrate solution by copper: write the reaction2 marks

Given: copper metal is added to silver nitrate solution and silver is recovered. Asked: the equation.

Concept used: displacement — copper is more reactive than silver, so it displaces silver (Topic 6). Why it applies: a free metal is placed in a solution of a less reactive metal's compound.

  1. 1

    Reactants: copper (Cu) and silver nitrate (AgNOX3\ce{AgNO3}AgNOX3​).

  2. 2

    Copper takes silver's place → copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NOX3)X2\ce{Cu(NO3)2}Cu(NOX3​)X2​ (Cu valency 2), and free silver.

  3. 3

    Skeletal: Cu+AgNOX3→Cu(NOX3)X2+Ag\ce{Cu + AgNO3 -> Cu(NO3)2 + Ag}Cu+AgNOX3​​Cu(NOX3​)X2​+Ag. Nitrate: 1 | 2.

  4. 4

    Put 2 in front of AgNOX3\ce{AgNO3}AgNOX3​ → nitrate 2 | 2, but now Ag 2 | 1.

  5. 5

    Put 2 in front of Ag → Ag 2 | 2.

  6. Check: Cu 1 | 1; Ag 2 | 2; N 2 | 2; O 6 | 6 ✔. Copper is above silver on the ladder, so the reaction is possible ✔.

  7. Answer Cu(s)+2 AgNOX3(aq)→Cu(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 Ag(s)\ce{Cu(s) + 2AgNO3(aq) -> Cu(NO3)2(aq) + 2Ag(s)}Cu(s)+2AgNOX3​(aq)​Cu(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2Ag(s) — a displacement reaction.

    Common trap: Writing CuNOX3\ce{CuNO3}CuNOX3​. Copper here forms copper(II) nitrate, Cu(NOX3)X2\ce{Cu(NO3)2}Cu(NOX3​)X2​.
Exercise Q15What is a precipitation reaction? Explain with examples.2 marks

Given: — Asked: a definition with examples.

Concept used: precipitate = insoluble solid formed from solutions (Topic 6). Why it applies: the name of the reaction comes from the solid it produces.

  1. 1

    When two solutions are mixed and an insoluble solid forms, that solid is a precipitate.

  2. 2

    A reaction that produces a precipitate is a precipitation reaction.

  3. 3

    Example 1 (white precipitate of barium sulphate):

    NaX2SOX4(aq)+BaClX2(aq)→BaSOX4(s)+2 NaCl(aq)\ce{Na2SO4(aq) + BaCl2(aq) -> BaSO4(s) + 2NaCl(aq)}NaX2​SOX4​(aq)+BaClX2​(aq)​BaSOX4​(s)+2NaCl(aq)Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Example 2 (yellow precipitate of lead iodide):

    Pb(NOX3)X2(aq)+2 KI(aq)→PbIX2(s)+2 KNOX3(aq)\ce{Pb(NO3)2(aq) + 2KI(aq) -> PbI2(s) + 2KNO3(aq)}Pb(NOX3​)X2​(aq)+2KI(aq)​PbIX2​(s)+2KNOX3​(aq)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: in each example the reactants are (aq) and exactly one product is (s) — the precipitate ✔.

  6. Answer A precipitation reaction is one in which an insoluble solid (precipitate) forms when solutions react — e.g. white barium sulphate and yellow lead iodide, as above.

    Common trap: Calling any reaction with a solid product "precipitation". The solid must form from solutions and not dissolve.
Exercise Q16Explain oxidation and reduction in terms of oxygen, with two examples each3 marks

Given: — Asked: both terms in terms of gain or loss of oxygen, with two examples each.

Concept used: oxidation = gain of oxygen; reduction = loss of oxygen (Topic 7). Why it applies: the question restricts us to the oxygen definitions.

  1. 1

    (a) Oxidation — gain of oxygen by a substance

    2 Cu+OX2→heat2 CuO\ce{2Cu + O2 ->[\text{heat}] 2CuO}2Cu+OX2​heat​2CuO: copper gains oxygen → copper is oxidised.

  2. 2

    C+OX2→COX2\ce{C + O2 -> CO2}C+OX2​​COX2​: carbon gains oxygen → carbon is oxidised.

  3. 1

    (b) Reduction — loss of oxygen by a substance

    CuO+HX2→heatCu+HX2O\ce{CuO + H2 ->[\text{heat}] Cu + H2O}CuO+HX2​heat​Cu+HX2​O: copper(II) oxide loses oxygen → CuO\ce{CuO}CuO is reduced.

  4. 2

    ZnO+C→Zn+CO\ce{ZnO + C -> Zn + CO}ZnO+C​Zn+CO: zinc oxide loses oxygen → ZnO\ce{ZnO}ZnO is reduced.

  5. Check: all four equations are balanced, and in each we named the reactant that gained or lost oxygen ✔.

  6. Answer Oxidation = gain of oxygen (e.g. Cu → CuO; C → COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​). Reduction = loss of oxygen (e.g. CuO → Cu; ZnO → Zn).

    Common trap: Giving a reaction without saying which substance is oxidised or reduced.
Exercise Q17A shiny brown element X turns black when heated in air. Name X and the black compound.2 marks

Given: X is a shiny brown element; heated in air, it turns black. Asked: X and the black compound.

Concept used: heating a metal in air oxidises it (Topic 7). Why it applies: heating in air supplies oxygen.

  1. 1

    A shiny, reddish-brown metal is copper.

  2. 2

    Heated in air, copper combines with oxygen.

  3. 3

    The product, copper(II) oxide, is black:

    2 Cu(s)+OX2(g)→heat2 CuO(s)\ce{2Cu(s) + O2(g) ->[\text{heat}] 2CuO(s)}2Cu(s)+OX2​(g)heat​2CuO(s)Swipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: Cu 2 | 2, O 2 | 2 ✔; the colours (brown metal → black oxide) match the question ✔.

  5. Answer X = copper (Cu); the black compound is copper(II) oxide (CuO\ce{CuO}CuO).

    Common trap: Answering "iron" — iron is grey, and its rust is reddish-brown, not black.
Exercise Q18Why do we paint iron articles?2 marks

Given: iron articles such as gates and grills are painted. Asked: why.

Concept used: rusting needs both oxygen and moisture (Topic 7). Why it applies: paint changes what can reach the iron surface.

  1. 1

    Iron rusts when it is exposed to oxygen and moisture in the air.

  2. 2

    Rusting slowly eats away the iron and weakens it (corrosion).

  3. 3

    A coat of paint covers the surface.

  4. 4

    Air and moisture can no longer reach the iron, so it does not rust.

  5. Check: where paint chips off an old gate, rust appears first — consistent with this reason ✔.

  6. Answer To prevent rusting. Paint forms a protective layer that keeps oxygen and moisture away from the iron.

    Common trap: Writing "to make it look nice". Appearance is a bonus; the scientific reason is preventing corrosion.
Exercise Q19Why are oil- and fat-containing foods flushed with nitrogen?2 marks

Given: packets of oily food are filled with nitrogen. Asked: why.

Concept used: rancidity is the oxidation of fats and oils (Topic 7). Why it applies: removing oxygen removes the cause of rancidity.

  1. 1

    Fats and oils react with oxygen in air and get oxidised.

  2. 2

    This makes them rancid — their smell and taste change.

  3. 3

    Nitrogen is an unreactive gas; filling the packet with it pushes out the oxygen.

  4. 4

    Without oxygen, the fats and oils are not oxidised, so the food stays fresh longer.

  5. Check: an opened packet goes stale within days, a sealed nitrogen-filled one lasts months — consistent with oxygen being the cause ✔.

  6. Answer To prevent rancidity. Nitrogen replaces the oxygen in the packet, so the fats and oils are not oxidised.

    Common trap: Writing "nitrogen kills germs". Nitrogen's job is to keep oxygen out.
Exercise Q20Explain corrosion and rancidity, with one example each3 marks

Given: — Asked: meaning of each term, with one example each.

Concept used: both are everyday effects of oxidation (Topic 7). Why it applies: in each case a substance reacts with oxygen in the air.

  1. 1

    (a) Corrosion

    Meaning: the slow damage of a metal's surface by things in its surroundings — oxygen, moisture, acids.

  2. 2

    Example: rusting of iron — iron left in moist air gets a reddish-brown coating of rust (hydrated iron(III) oxide). (Others: black coating on silver; green coating on copper.)

  3. 1

    (b) Rancidity

    Meaning: the oxidation of fats and oils in food by air, which spoils their smell and taste.

  4. 2

    Example: chips, namkeen or butter kept open for a long time develop a stale, unpleasant smell and taste.

  5. Check: both examples involve exposure to air (oxygen), which matches both being oxidation ✔.

  6. Answer Corrosion: a metal slowly damaged by oxygen, moisture or acids around it, e.g. rusting of iron. Rancidity: oxidation of fats and oils that spoils smell and taste, e.g. stale chips.

    Common trap: Defining rancidity as "food going bad due to bacteria". It is oxidation.

Group Activity

Group Activity (p.16)Four beakers: which changes are exothermic and which are endothermic?3 marks

Set-up (paraphrased): beakers A, B, C contain water; beaker D contains copper sulphate solution. Temperatures are recorded. Then potassium sulphate is added to A, ammonium nitrate to B, anhydrous copper sulphate to C and fine iron filings to D, and the final temperatures are recorded.

Given: four mixtures and their starting temperatures. Asked: which changes are exothermic and which are endothermic.

Concept used: temperature rises → heat released → exothermic; temperature falls → heat absorbed → endothermic (Topic 4, Topic 5). Why it applies: the only measurement taken is the change in temperature.

  1. •

    Steps to reach the answer:

  2. 1

    Record the starting temperature of each liquid.

  3. 2

    Add the substance, stir, and record the final temperature.

  4. 3

    If final > initial, heat was given out → exothermic.

  5. 4

    If final < initial, heat was taken in → endothermic.

    Predicted results

    Beaker What is added Expected temperature change Exothermic or endothermic? Why
    A potassium sulphate to water falls by about 1–3 °C endothermic Dissolving potassium sulphate absorbs heat from the water.
    B ammonium nitrate to water falls clearly (the beaker feels cold) endothermic Dissolving ammonium nitrate absorbs a lot of heat — this is how "instant cold packs" work.
    C anhydrous copper sulphate (white) to water rises exothermic The white powder combines with water (it turns blue) and releases heat.
    D iron filings to copper sulphate solution rises (slightly) exothermic A displacement reaction takes place and releases heat: Fe(s)+CuSOX4(aq)→FeSOX4(aq)+Cu(s)\ce{Fe(s) + CuSO4(aq) -> FeSO4(aq) + Cu(s)}Fe(s)+CuSOX4​(aq)​FeSOX4​(aq)+Cu(s). The blue colour fades and reddish-brown copper forms.

  6. Check: two beakers warm up and two cool down; each "why" agrees with its temperature change ✔.

  7. Answer Exothermic: C and D. Endothermic: A and B.

    Points to note:

    • A and B are dissolving processes (physical changes with a heat change). In C, white anhydrous copper sulphate combines with water to form blue hydrated copper sulphate (a combination that releases heat). D is a displacement reaction. Teachers may ask you to point this out.
    • Use the same volume of water in each beaker for a fair comparison.
    • Safety: do not taste or touch the chemicals with bare hands; wash your hands afterwards.
    Common trap: Assuming every substance that dissolves in water warms it up. Some (like ammonium nitrate) cool it down.
